name: Stewardship of Time, Talent, and the Body

objectives.text: Identify time, abilities, and our bodies as good gifts from God who made us
Recall from Psalm 139 that God formed each person's body and made it wonderfully
Describe everyday ways to care for the body God made, such as sleeping, eating well, washing, and playing actively
Retell the parable of the talents and explain that God expects us to use what He gives us faithfully
State the fourth commandment and describe the pattern of six days of work and one day of rest that God set at creation
Explain why the Reformed tradition keeps the first day of the week as the Lord's Day and describe activities that keep it holy
Explain what Paul means by making the best use of the time by reading Ephesians 5:15-16 in its context
Describe the difference between diligence and laziness using the wisdom of Proverbs
Explain from 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 why the Reformed tradition teaches that a believer's body belongs to God and is a temple of the Holy Spirit
Identify the spiritual gifts listed in the New Testament and explain that they are given to serve others in the church
Distinguish busyness from fruitfulness using the accounts of Martha and Mary and the vine and the branches
Explain how the sixth commandment requires lawful care of one's own life and forbids harming one's own body
Apply the principle of doing all to the glory of God to choices about eating, drinking, sleep, work, and recreation
Analyze Psalm 90 to explain how the brevity of life calls for wise use of time
Analyze Jesus' Sabbath controversies to explain the tradition's teaching that works of necessity and mercy are fitting on the Lord's Day
Explain biblical teaching against gluttony and drunkenness as misuse of the body and identify self-control as fruit of the Spirit
Interpret Romans 6 and Romans 12 to explain how the body is to be presented as an instrument of righteousness and an act of worship
Explain how Sabbath rest expresses dependence on God's provision and points to the rest fulfilled in Christ
Explain how Paul grounds sexual purity in the truth that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit
Identify personal abilities and propose specific ways to use them in service to the church and neighbor
Compare the biblical teaching that gifts are given for the common good with attitudes that treat gifts as marks of status or reasons for envy
Construct a weekly schedule that balances work, worship, rest, service, and care for the body and justify its choices from Scripture
Evaluate habits of technology and entertainment use as matters of time stewardship using biblical principles
Evaluate the idolatry of health and appearance against neglect of the body using Paul's teaching on bodily training and false asceticism
Defend the goodness of the physical body against Gnostic views using the doctrines of creation, incarnation, and resurrection
Explain the historic Reformed position on the cessation of revelatory gifts and the continuing call to use ordinary gifts
Analyze how the hope of bodily resurrection shapes the present stewardship of the body and of one's labor
Evaluate approaches to self-discipline in light of the Reformed teaching that holy living flows from grace rather than earning God's favor

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (time as gift, body as temple, using gifts, redeeming the time, Sabbath rest, busyness vs fruitfulness, Psalm 90, instrument of righteousness, rest and trust, spiritual gifts, weekly schedule, health idolatry vs neglect, anti-Gnostic defense, discipline and grace). Recast 'Observe resting on the Sabbath' as describing Lord's Day practice, and dropped 'Explain why we shouldn't waste our lives' and 'Identify healthy habits as worship' as vague, replacing them with diligence vs laziness from Proverbs and applying 1 Corinthians 10:31 to daily choices. Added missing competencies: God forming the body, the parable of the talents, the fourth commandment and creation pattern, works of necessity and mercy, sixth-commandment care of one's own life, gluttony and drunkenness, sexual purity grounded in the body as temple, gifts for the common good, technology and entertainment, the Reformed view on cessation of revelatory gifts, and resurrection hope shaping stewardship. Anchored each objective to specific verses and to the Westminster Standards and Heidelberg Catechism where they state the doctrine. Left money, vocation, and marriage to the sibling sub-topics.
